newsitem.title: USA: FEATURE - U.S. insurers look to active year.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE - U.S. insurers look to active year.

text.p: U.S. personal property insurers appear poised for a pick up in merger and acquisition activity in 1997 after sitting out most of last year's record-setting action.

The life and health insurance sectors are likely to remain hotbeds of deal-making activity, and more foreign buyers may emerge in 1997 as they seek to expand their presence in the important U.S. market, industry sources say.

The insurance industry overall is likely to keep Wall Street nearly as busy this year as it was in 1996, when a record 281 deals valued at $23.1 billion were announced. That compares with 247 deals valued at $24.9 billion in 1995, according to Securities Data Co.

Some of the year's biggest property-casualty deals included the sale of Aetna's property-casualty business to Travelers Group Inc for $4 billion and the purchase of American Re Corp by Germany's Munich Re for $3.3 billion.

In the life insurance sector, the Dutch Aegon NV group agreed to buy the life insurance business of Providian Corp in a deal worth about $3.5 billion. General Electric Co's GE Capital Corp bought First Colony Corp for $1.8 billion and Provident Cos Inc agreed to buy Paul Revere Corp for $1.2 billion.
And in the insurance brokerage sector, Aon Corp agreed to buy Alexander & Alexander Services Inc for about $1.23 billion.
POTENTIALLY LARGE DEALS IN PIPELINE
But more, potentially large deals are in the pipeline, some Wall Street bankers said.
"There are certainly significant transactions in the financial institutions sector percolating," said James MacNaughton, head of the financial institutions group at Salomon Brothers.
"If the financial markets continue to be attractive to people who need to raise money, there will be a plethora of deals," he said.
Deals expected in 1997 include the sale of Chubb Corp's life insurance business and the sale of at least some of Xerox Corp's property-casualty insurance businesses.

Kohlberg Kravis & Roberts had agreed to buy Xerox's Talegen insurance businesses in January 1996 for about $2.7 billion, but the deal fell apart in September, leaving Xerox in search of new buyers for the five units.
Meanwhile, CIGNA Corp and Prudential Insurance Co of America are expected to give serious thought to the future of their health insurance businesses.
"You can assume they are actively considering whether they want to get bigger or smaller," one investment banker said. "That would also include companies that have already made big acquisitions."
Aetna Inc, after selling its property-casualty business this year, bought U.S. Healthcare Inc for $8.9 billion.
And The Hartford, which has a new chief executive this year, may consider reshaping its multi-line businesses as well.
PROPERTY-CASUALTY AREA TO SEE MOST ACTIVITY
But it is the property-casualty sector, especially the personal lines business, that is likely to see the biggest increase in the level of merger activity.

"I think you're going to see a continuation of the activity in the life area and then I think you're going to see, frankly, more activity in the primary property-casualty area," said Robert Goodman, managing director in charge of the insurance group at Wasserstein Perella.

So far, most of the property-casualty deals have arisen from special, distressed situations or they came from the reinsurance industry, which is further along in its consolidation, said Eric Simpson, senior vice-president at A.M. Best.
But the new, increased activity will come as some of the broad-based changes taking place in the life insurance industry finally catch up to the overall property-casualty sector, Simpson said.

Insurers in the personal lines and small commercial businesses will be among those to feel the most pressure from the years of slow growth, pricing pressure and increasing competition from rivals with new, cheaper distribution systems, he said.
Old, entrenched managements also will be forced to reconsider mergers as they come under increasing pressure to boost the performances of their companies in this slow-growth environment, he said.
"We believe M&A activity is just beginning to take off for property-casualty," Simpson added.
An excess of capital also will contribute, said Alan Levin, director of insurance rating services at Standard & Poor's.

"The capitalisation of the industry is in pretty good shape, both because of the lack of any huge catastrophe and the run-up in the stock market," he said. "People have money and they can't grow by selling so they'll grow by acquiring blocks of business or companies."
Property-casualty sectors ripe for consolidation include certain niche sectors such as the medical malpractice business and possibly the non-standard auto insurance business, Simpson said.
REINSURANCE MERGERS MAY SLOW
But reinsurance mergers may slow after a flurry of deals among the biggest companies in 1996, said Wasserstein's Goodman.

Last year, General Re Corp bought National Re Corp for $940 million, Switzerland's Swiss Reinsurance Co bought Britain's Mercantile & General Re for about $2.27 billion and Munich Re bought American Re for about $3.3 billion.
Munich Re was just one of several foreign insurers seeking to acquire U.S. insurers in 1996 and interest from overseas is likely to increase.
"There are a group of substantial European financial institutions who would like a more important position in the United States market," said Salomon's MacNaughton.
These financial institutions, he said, are interested in expanding their principal European businesses as well as diversifying into other financial businesses.
Other foreign insurers believed to be interested in U.S. deals include the Dutch Internationale Nederlanden Groep NV, Germany's Allianz AG Holding and France's Axa SA, sources said.
U.S. insurers also could see a new kind of buyer in 1997 -- banks.
"We hear from certain banking executives now, primarily on the life side," said one investment banker.

With the potential for further deregulation in the U.S. financial services industry, such mergers may just be a matter of time, said Mark Puccia, director of Standard & Poor's insurance rating services.
Whether such mergers would take place in 1997, he said, was "a wild card".
But, "that's the big bang out there that would change the landscape dramatically," he added.
